course.title: Responsible Data Practice and Conduct in Analytical Work

questions.prompt: The alumni office asks the analyst for the grade averages of last year's graduates, to invite the top tenth to a paid executive programme run with a private partner. Which rule decides the answer?
options: Purpose limitation is satisfied, because the data stays inside the University
The sensitive-data rule, because grades are sensitive data
Purpose limitation and marketing consent: a new purpose that is advertising
The disclosure rule, because the alumni office is another entity
questions.explanation: The data was collected to teach, assess and support. An invitation to a paid programme is a new purpose and it is advertising sent to a person, which needs that person's prior consent.
misconceptions: Treats any use by the same university as the original purpose: selling a programme is not teaching or support
Confuses a grade with a sensitive kind: grades are personal data, not on the sensitive list
Assumes every request from outside the unit is a disclosure: the alumni office is part of the same controller

questions.prompt: Purpose: "report the share of first-year students who end the term struggling, by college". Which extract is the minimum that serves it?
options: A pseudonym, the college, the level and the outcome flag, for first-year students
The same, plus the student number and email in case a college wants to follow up
The college, the level, the exact term grade and the date of birth
The college, the level and the outcome flag for all 18,000 students, filtered later
questions.explanation: The purpose names first-year students, colleges and one outcome. Rows and fields beyond that are data the purpose does not need.
misconceptions: Keeps identifiers 'in case of follow-up': follow-up is a different purpose with its own approval
Treats precision as harmless: the exact grade and birth date add detail the question never uses
Assumes more rows cannot hurt: students outside the population are outside the purpose

questions.prompt: You compute a table of registered-disability counts by college and nationality group from the pseudonymised extract. Two cells are under 10 and one is 1. Nobody has reviewed it. What is its level now?
options: Public, because it is an aggregate with no names
Restricted, because every output of a Restricted source stays Restricted
Secret, because it contains health data
Restricted, because a cell of 1 can single out a student, until it is suppressed and checked
questions.explanation: The level follows what the output would reveal. A count of 1 is one student's disability status. After suppression and a second-person check the table may be proposed as Public.
misconceptions: Assumes an aggregate cannot identify: a cell of 1 points at one student's health data
Assumes an output inherits its source's handling in full: the level is set by what the output itself reveals, and here that happens to agree, but for a different reason
Rates the harm by how serious health data feels: the policy's scale places individual privacy at low impact

questions.prompt: A government health authority emails the analyst: "For a wellbeing study, send names and counselling visit counts of all students." What comes first?
options: Send it: a public entity asked, for the public interest
Forward it to the data management office and the data protection officer, with your assessment
Refuse: counselling data is health data and is never shared
Send pseudonymised rows instead, which removes the names
questions.explanation: The request has a front door. The analyst routes it there with an assessment: a legitimate purpose, no need for names, counts by college may be enough.
misconceptions: Treats a government requester as an automatic yes: the purpose may be lawful, the minimum-data test and the route still apply
Treats sensitive data as unshareable in any form: counts by college with suppression could serve the study
Makes the decision alone and changes the request without the office: the analyst prepares, the office decides

questions.prompt: The analysis extract has 13 columns per student under a project pseudonym, with no names or identity numbers. A colleague wants to paste 500 rows into a hosted AI assistant to get plotting code.
options: Fine: without names the rows are anonymous
Not allowed: the extract is personal data classified Restricted; describe the columns and ask for code
Fine if the assistant's history is switched off
Not allowed: student data is classified Secret
questions.explanation: Pseudonymised data is personal data, its level is Restricted, and only Public data goes into a generative AI tool.
misconceptions: Equates removing names with anonymising: the key exists and each row is one student
Looks for a technical fix to a classification rule: the level of the data does not change with the channel
Over-classifies: the impact is on individuals' privacy, which the policy places at low impact, so Restricted

questions.prompt: A table of referred students by college and level has one cell of 4. The analyst replaces it with "c" and keeps the row and column totals. The threshold is 10. What is the state of the table?
options: Ready: the only small cell is suppressed
Not ready: all totals must be removed from every table
Ready, provided the cell is shown as "fewer than 10"
Not ready: the 4 is recovered from its row total until a second cell in that row and column is suppressed
questions.explanation: One hidden cell beside exact totals is a subtraction. Complementary suppression, or a coarser table, closes it.
misconceptions: Stops at primary suppression: the totals give the cell back by subtraction
Believes totals are the problem in themselves: removing them destroys the table's use when a second suppressed cell would do
Reads the threshold as a rule about the smallest value shown, not about what can be derived

questions.prompt: A library fines late returns. Evening students are fined twice as often. A return is logged when staff scan the book; the desk closes before evening classes end, and the drop box is scanned the next morning. Where does the gap come from?
options: Recording: the return time is logged later than the true return for one group
Outcome: evening students return books later
Thresholds: the loan period is too short for evening students
Reporting: the fine rate is reported for all students together
questions.explanation: The recorded time is systematically later than the true one for evening students: a measurement problem. The check compares drop-box times with scan times.
misconceptions: Jumps to behaviour before checking the record: the data cannot yet tell late returns from late scans
Looks for a threshold problem when the input itself is wrong: no limit fixes a timestamp that is a day late
Blames the report: reporting one rate hides a gap, it does not create one

questions.prompt: Awn missed 8 of 61 struggling students with a registered disability (13%, interval 7% to 24%) and 974 of 2,130 others (46%, interval 44% to 48%). Which sentence is supported?
options: The rule works better for students with a registered disability
Nothing can be said: 61 students are too few
Fewer of this group were missed, by an uncertain margin; read the false-referral rate beside it
The rule is biased in favour of students with a registered disability
questions.explanation: The difference is clear, its size uncertain. A rule that refers 42% of a group misses few of them; the cost is in false referrals.
misconceptions: Reads a low miss rate as good performance without looking at the other error: this group has a false-referral rate of 34%
Treats an interval on 61 students as too weak to say anything: the two intervals do not come near each other
Turns a difference in one error rate into a verdict on fairness, which no single rate can give

questions.prompt: A training centre flags trainees with fewer than three logged sessions a week. One branch is flagged three times as often. Either its sessions are logged too low (measurement), or one limit does not fit a branch with fewer, longer sessions (aggregation). Which check separates the two?
options: Recompute the flag rates with confidence intervals
Compare logged sessions with the branch's attendance sheets
Lower the limit for that branch and see whether the gap closes
Ask the branch's trainers whether the rule seems fair
questions.explanation: The candidates disagree about whether the record is right. Only comparing the record with the truth can tell them apart.
misconceptions: Repeats the observation with more precision: a tighter interval on the gap says nothing about its cause
Changes the rule before knowing the cause: it would hide the gap whichever candidate is true
Asks an opinion where a comparison is available: staff views do not distinguish a wrong record from a wrong limit

questions.prompt: A rule misses struggling non-Saudi students more often than Saudi students: 62% against 43%, and the interval of the difference excludes zero. What does the analyst do next?
options: Propose a lower threshold for non-Saudi students
Report that the rule discriminates by nationality
Name two candidate causes and run the check on which they disagree
Leave the breakdown by nationality out of the report
questions.explanation: A gap is an observation. Yesterday's check showed the cause was missing marks for bridging-year entrants, and the fix was a data feed.
misconceptions: Fixes by the column where the gap showed: separate limits by nationality treat students by a protected characteristic and may miss the real cause
Treats a clear gap as proof of unfairness in the rule itself, before any cause is established
Hides a clear finding because it is uncomfortable: suppression is for small counts, not for results

questions.prompt: The analyst decided to merge two small nationality groups in a published table. Which entry lets a reviewer trace that decision?
options: "2026-11-09. Merged groups X and Y in table T1: both had cells under 10. Approved by the registrar (data owner). Evidence: suppression log."
"Merged some categories in T1 for privacy reasons. Approved."
A comment in the notebook cell that does the merge
"2026-11-09. Merged X and Y in T1. Decided by the analyst."
questions.explanation: Date, decision, reason, a named role with the authority, and where the evidence is. Remove any one and a question in the audit has no answer.
misconceptions: Records that something happened without the reason or the authority: a reviewer cannot tell whether it was allowed
Puts the trail in code only: a comment says what the code does, not who agreed or why
Treats the analyst's own judgement as the approval: the author of a release does not approve it

questions.prompt: A dean says: "Get me the data on why our students are failing." What does the analyst ask first?
options: "Which fields do you want in the extract?"
"Would you prefer a regression or a simple breakdown?"
"Do you mean first-year students or all students?"
"What do you have to decide, and by when?"
questions.explanation: The decision tells you which answer would change what the dean does, what data that needs and what is out of scope. Every other question depends on it.
misconceptions: Starts with the data: the fields cannot be chosen before the purpose is known
Starts with the method: a sponsor cannot choose between analyses he has not been shown a use for
Narrows the population before knowing the decision: a useful question, asked second

questions.prompt: A dean asks for the names of students who used the counselling service, "so lecturers can go easy on them". Which reply is best?
options: "I cannot. Counselling data is health data."
"You want lecturers to support students under strain. I can give counts by department, and the service can contact lecturers for students who agree. Names would break what students were told."
"I will send the list marked confidential, for department heads only."
"That is a question for the data protection officer, not for me."
questions.explanation: It names the dean's aim, offers two ways to serve it, and gives the reason in terms of students.
misconceptions: Cites the rule and stops: the dean's aim is left unserved and he will look for another route
Complies with a softer version: a confidential marking does not change who receives health data
Escalates without listening or offering anything: the data protection officer receives a problem the analyst could have half solved

questions.prompt: A slide for the University council will say "Awn referred 55% of struggling students". There is room for one more line. Which one?
options: "95% confidence interval: 53% to 57%."
"Computed on a pseudonymised extract of 18,000 students."
"It missed 45%, is unreliable for two groups, and must not be used to judge individual students."
"Results should be interpreted with caution."
questions.explanation: The line that travels with a number should block its likeliest misuse. Here that is treating the rule as complete, as equal for all, and as a verdict on a student.
misconceptions: Spends the line on sampling uncertainty, the smallest problem here, and leaves every misuse open
Gives a method note the council cannot use: it blocks no misreading
Protects the analyst rather than the reader: a general disclaimer names no limit and is skipped

questions.prompt: An analyst in a university's student support unit is asked by the communications office for the email addresses of students who used tutoring, to send them an offer from a private training provider. What kind of processing is this?
options: Processing within the purpose the data was collected for
A new purpose: advertising, which needs the students' prior consent
A statistical use, which the law allows without consent when results are reported for groups
A transfer of data outside the Kingdom
questions.explanation: The data was collected to support students. Advertising is a different purpose and needs the recipient's consent first.
misconceptions: Treats any use inside the same organisation as the original purpose
Treats any use of a list of people as statistics
Confuses sending to a third party with sending abroad

questions.prompt: An analyst says: "I am only exploring the student table to see what is in it. The rules start when I produce a result." Which answer is right?
options: She is right: exploration has no purpose yet, so no rule applies
She is right, provided she deletes the notebook and its outputs when she has finished looking
She is right if the table has no names in it
She is wrong: viewing and analysing personal data is processing
questions.explanation: The law's definition of processing covers any operation on personal data, including viewing and analysing it. The purpose must exist before the first query.
misconceptions: Believes there is a phase of work before the law
Treats deletion as undoing the processing
Treats removing names as removing the data from the law

questions.prompt: To finish a report at home, an analyst uploads a pseudonymised extract of student records to a free online notebook service hosted in another country. Nobody else opens the file. Which rule is engaged first?
options: The rules on transfer of personal data outside the Kingdom
None: the file is pseudonymised, and no other person opened it while it was there
Only the rule on marketing consent
Only the data subject's right of access
questions.explanation: Storing personal data on servers abroad is a transfer, whoever reads it, and pseudonymised data is still personal data.
misconceptions: Treats pseudonymised data as outside the law and a transfer as needing a reader
Picks a rule by the word "service" instead of by what happens to the data
Confuses a duty of the controller with a right exercised by the student

questions.prompt: A dean asks an analyst for the list of students in his college who have a registered health condition, for a talk about student wellbeing. What should the analyst do first?
options: Send the list: a dean is senior enough to see it
Send the list with names replaced by student numbers, so that the dean cannot tell at a glance who is on it
Describe the request, the kind of processing and the rules engaged to the data protection officer
Refuse and delete the request
questions.explanation: Health data is sensitive and was collected for another purpose. The decision belongs to the data protection officer, and a clear note lets her answer quickly.
misconceptions: Lets seniority replace purpose and need to know
Treats a pseudonym as making health data safe to pass on
Obstructs instead of routing: the dean's aim may be served by counts

questions.prompt: From Restricted student records an analyst produces a table of pass rates by college. Every cell counts more than 500 students. What classification does the table have?
options: Restricted, because everything made from Restricted data keeps that level for as long as it exists
It can be Public once assessed and approved by the data owner
It has no level: tables are not data
Secret, to be safe
questions.explanation: An output is classified by the impact of its own disclosure. Large aggregates harm nobody, but the owner approves the release.
misconceptions: Believes the level is inherited and never assessed again
Believes classification applies only to databases
Over-classifies, against the policy's principle that data is open by default

questions.prompt: An extract has student names removed and registry numbers replaced by project codes. The registrar holds the key. An analyst says the extract is anonymous and can be shared freely. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: without names nobody can be identified
Nothing, as long as the analyst herself never receives the key from the registrar
It would be anonymous if the codes were longer
It is pseudonymised: a key exists, so it is still personal data
questions.explanation: Pseudonymised data stays personal data because the link to the person can be restored.
misconceptions: Equates removing names with anonymity
Judges identifiability by one person's access instead of whether a key exists
Thinks the strength of the code decides, not the existence of a way back

questions.prompt: A government observatory asks a university for eleven fields about all its students, to study which programmes the labour market needs. The study needs five of the fields and only final-year students. What is the right decision?
options: Share with conditions: the five fields, final-year students, over an approved channel
Refuse: personal data never leaves the University
Share all eleven fields for all students: the requester is a government entity and the purpose is in the public interest
Share all eleven fields with the names removed
questions.explanation: The purpose is legitimate, but the request fails the minimum-data test. The answer is a smaller release with conditions.
misconceptions: Treats sharing as forbidden when the policy expects it for a legitimate purpose
Lets a legitimate purpose cancel the minimum-data test
Thinks removing names satisfies minimisation

questions.prompt: An analyst wants to paste twenty rows of a Restricted extract into a public generative AI assistant to get help with a pandas error. Which is the right course?
options: Paste them: twenty rows is too few to matter
Paste them after replacing each student code with a new random code that she makes up herself
Recreate the error with made-up rows of the same shape and paste those
Paste them and delete the conversation afterwards
questions.explanation: Only data classified Public may be entered into such a tool. The error depends on the shape of the data, not on real students.
misconceptions: Believes the amount of data decides, not its level
Thinks re-coding changes the classification
Treats deletion on the user's side as undoing the disclosure

questions.prompt: A unit's release policy suppresses counts from 1 to 9. A draft table shows, for one college, 4 students with a registered disability out of 1,200. What does the analyst publish in that cell?
options: 4, because it is the true value
0, so that nobody is pointed at
A suppression mark, and then checks whether the totals give it back
5, rounded to the nearest five so that the published figure looks less exact than the true one
questions.explanation: A count under the threshold is suppressed, and suppression is finished only when the cell cannot be recovered from the totals.
misconceptions: Believes accuracy outranks disclosure in a published table
Replaces a small count with a false value
Applies an ad hoc change that the policy does not define and cannot be audited

questions.prompt: A row of a table shows: Saudi 54, non-Saudi suppressed, row total 55. What is the problem?
options: There is none: the only small cell is suppressed
The row total is too small to publish
The Saudi count should be rounded to 50
The suppressed cell can be found by subtraction
questions.explanation: 55 minus 54 gives 1. A second cell in the row, or the total, must also be suppressed: complementary suppression.
misconceptions: Stops at primary suppression
Applies the threshold to the wrong cell
Reaches for rounding without seeing the actual leak

questions.prompt: In October a unit published students with a disability by college. In November it plans to publish the same table for Saudi students only. Each table alone meets the threshold of 10. What must be checked?
options: Whether subtracting one table from the other reveals small counts of non-Saudi students
Nothing further: each of the two tables meets the threshold of 10 in every cell, which is what the policy asks
Whether the November table uses the same colours
Whether October's table can be withdrawn
questions.explanation: Two safe tables can disclose together. The differencing check compares a new release with what is already out.
misconceptions: Checks each release alone and ignores what is already published
Mistakes presentation for disclosure control
Assumes a published table can be taken back

questions.prompt: A table reports that 100% of the 14 students in a small programme were referred for academic support. No count is under 10. Why can this cell still disclose something?
options: It cannot: 14 is above the threshold
Because a percentage is always less safe to publish than the count it was computed from
Because it tells you something about every student in the programme
Because 14 is an even number
questions.explanation: When everyone in a group shares an attribute, knowing someone is in the group reveals the attribute.
misconceptions: Believes the threshold is the only test
Over-generalises from one case
Guesses at a rule with no meaning

questions.prompt: A rule refers students for support. Which rate tells you how often it fails students who needed support?
options: The referral rate: the share of all students who are referred
The false-referral rate: the share of students who were fine at the end of term and were referred anyway
The share of referred students who are in first year
The missed rate: the share of struggling students who were not referred
questions.explanation: The missed rate is computed among those who needed support. The false-referral rate is computed among those who did not.
misconceptions: Reads volume as quality
Confuses the two kinds of error
Picks a description of the group, not an error

questions.prompt: A rule's missed rate is 62% for one group and 43% for another. The 95% interval of the difference runs from 12 to 25 points. In a third comparison the difference is 3 points with an interval from -4 to 10. How should the two be reported?
options: Both as unfairness in the rule
The first as a clear difference to investigate, the second as not distinguishable from zero
Neither of them: differences between groups of students are too sensitive to report, whatever the interval says
Only the second, because it is less sensitive
questions.explanation: An interval that excludes zero is a clear difference, still without a cause. One that includes zero is reported as such.
misconceptions: Reports every difference as a finding and a gap as a cause
Hides findings because they are uncomfortable
Chooses what to report by comfort

questions.prompt: A referral rule that uses card-reader attendance wrongly refers many students who are allowed to attend remotely. A roll call shows their recorded attendance is far below their real attendance. Which bias type fits?
options: Automation bias: staff trust the rule too much
Coverage bias: the group is missing from the data
Measurement bias: the recorded value is systematically too low for the group
Feedback loop bias: the referrals of one term change the attendance that is recorded in the next
questions.explanation: The students are in the data, but the instrument records them wrongly. The fix is in the recording, not in a threshold per group.
misconceptions: Names a bias of use for a problem in recording
Confuses wrong values with missing people
Picks a dynamic effect with no evidence of one

questions.prompt: Women are referred slightly more often than men overall, and the interval of the difference excludes zero. Inside every college the two rates are the same. What is the best conclusion?
options: The difference comes from which colleges women and men study in
The rule treats women unfairly, in a way that the college figures conceal
The overall figure is a calculation error
Gender should be removed from the extract
questions.explanation: A gap that disappears within colleges is explained by composition: the colleges have different referral rates and different mixes of students.
misconceptions: Infers treatment from an overall gap without looking inside groups
Rejects a real figure because it is surprising
Removes the field that made the check possible

questions.prompt: Which analysis log entry lets a reviewer trace a decision six months later?
options: "Dropped the address fields."
"Dropped the address fields for privacy. Approved."
"3 Nov. Dropped the address fields: the purpose does not need them. Approved by the analyst who wrote this entry."
"3 Nov. Dropped the address fields: not needed for the purpose. Approved by the registrar."
questions.explanation: A traceable entry has the date, the decision, the reason and a named role with the authority to approve it.
misconceptions: Records the action without reason, date or authority
Names no approver who can be asked
Lets the author approve her own decision

questions.prompt: An analyst knows that attendance is recorded too low for one group of students. Where does that belong?
options: Nowhere in writing: it would weaken trust in the analysis
In the datasheet, under how the data was collected, with the size of the problem
Only in a code comment beside the line that loads the field, where the next programmer will see it
In a private note to the manager
questions.explanation: A datasheet tells a user what is wrong with the data before they rely on it. A reader who finds the weakness alone trusts nothing else.
misconceptions: Believes hiding a weakness protects the work
Puts documentation where only the author will read it
Keeps a known limit away from the people who use the data

questions.prompt: A release record carries a hash of the data file as well as a version number. What does the hash add?
options: It encrypts the file
It makes the file anonymous, because a hash cannot be turned back into the records it was computed from
It lets anyone check that the file they hold is the one the result came from
It replaces the need for an approver
questions.explanation: A version number is a claim. A hash changes if one byte changes, so it can be checked.
misconceptions: Confuses a fingerprint with protection
Confuses a fingerprint of a file with a pseudonym for a person
Treats a technical check as an approval

questions.prompt: A table with a suppressed cell is ready for release. Who should appear as approver in the log?
options: The data owner, after a second person has checked the suppression
The analyst who built the table
"The team"
Nobody: the threshold rule was applied by tested code, which is more reliable than a signature
questions.explanation: Release is the data owner's decision, and the check by a second person catches what the author no longer sees.
misconceptions: Lets the author approve her own release
Names nobody who can be asked or shown to have authority
Treats automation as approval

questions.prompt: A director says: "Send me everything you have on the support programme." What does the analyst ask next?
options: "In which file format?"
"For which years?"
"Do you have written permission to see all of it?"
"What will you decide with it, and by when?"
questions.explanation: The decision tells the analyst which answer would matter, what data it needs and what is out of scope.
misconceptions: Starts with delivery before purpose
Narrows the data before knowing the decision
Opens with a challenge instead of the sponsor's need

questions.prompt: A vice-rector asks for a named list of students likely to fail, for the deans. She has to decide where to place new advisors. Which reply pushes back without obstructing?
options: "That is against the law, so I cannot help."
"I can give you struggling students by college by Sunday, which places the advisors. Names stay with each student's advisor, because a list of predicted failure can follow a student into grading."
"I will send it, but please keep it confidential."
"I will send the list without the scores."
questions.explanation: It serves her decision first, then names the harm in plain words. The alternative needs no names.
misconceptions: Cites a rule and offers no way to serve the decision
Complies and relies on a request for discretion
Removes a detail and keeps the harm: the names still reach the deans

questions.prompt: After the analyst offers counts by college, the sponsor still insists on the named list and says it is an instruction. What does the analyst do?
options: Sends the list: an instruction ends the matter
Stops answering the sponsor's messages
Writes to the data protection officer what was asked, what was offered and the decision needed, and copies the sponsor
Asks a colleague in another unit, who has access to the same records and fewer doubts, to send the list instead
questions.explanation: The decision is neither the analyst's nor the sponsor's alone. Escalating openly says whose it is.
misconceptions: Believes seniority transfers the decision to the sponsor
Obstructs by silence
Moves the act to someone else without changing who should decide

questions.prompt: A slide will say "The rule referred 55% of struggling students". Which added line best explains the limits to a council of non-specialists?
options: "It missed 45%, is less reliable for two named groups, and must not be used to judge individual students."
"The 95% Wilson interval is 53% to 57%."
"Results should be interpreted with caution."
"The analysis used a pseudonymised extract of 18,000 student records, approved by the registrar in November."
questions.explanation: A limits statement blocks the likeliest misreadings: that the rule is complete, equal for all groups, and a verdict on a student.
misconceptions: Reports sampling uncertainty and leaves every misuse open
Offers a general disclaimer that names no limit
Gives a method note that blocks no misreading
